implementation_notes: Union types are the closure in TypeScript: `type Payment = { kind: 'card'; number: string } | { kind: 'transfer'; iban: string }` is a fixed set, a literal-typed discriminant narrows the value inside `switch`/`if`, and assigning the residual value to `never` (or calling an `assertNever` helper) turns a missing case into a compile error; a `satisfies Record<Kind, T>` map (TS 4.9) checks exhaustiveness without a switch. `readonly` fields or `as const` factories supply the immutability half, and `strict`/`noImplicitReturns` make the guarantee meaningful. Types are erased at run time, so data from outside the program (API responses, JSON, storage) must be validated into the union before it can be trusted - the classic class hierarchy plus `instanceof` remains the alternative when cases carry behaviour and must interoperate with plain JavaScript classes.
pitfalls: Exhaustiveness exists only where `tsc` runs in strict mode: a `default: return ''` arm, or stripping types at runtime, removes the guarantee, and an `any`-typed value defeats it entirely.
Discriminant widening: building the object with a `string`-typed variable widens `kind`, so narrowing and the `never` check stop working - keep literals inline or use `as const`/`satisfies`.
Unions are structural and erased: an object with extra properties still satisfies a member, and `readonly` is compile-time only - a JavaScript caller can mutate the same object.
